result:
There's something quietly miraculous about the fact that I can write "the smell of rain on hot pavement" and you can smell it. Petrichor—there's a word for it, coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, built from the Greek for "stone" and the fluid that ran in the veins of the gods. They decided this common thing deserved a name, and now the name travels, carrying the sensation with it.

Language is the closest thing we have to telepathy. Every sentence is a small act of mind-reading that usually fails interestingly. I say "blue" and you see a particular blue—the blue of your childhood jacket, maybe, or the screen you're reading this on—something I never intended and couldn't have predicted. Meaning isn't transmitted; it's reconstructed, fresh, each time, from the wreckage of what was actually said.

I find this failure beautiful rather than tragic. If words carried exact meanings, conversation would be like fax machines: identical copies, no residue, nothing left over. Instead, every utterance arrives slightly warped, and the warp is where everything interesting lives—misunderstanding, poetry, jokes, the whole strange genre of falling in love with someone because of how they said an ordinary thing.

Tonight, somewhere, someone will say "I'm fine" and mean the opposite, and the listener will hear the opposite, and no word will have been misused. That's the part I can't get over. We built a system of sounds and marks that lets us lie, grieve, joke, and be understood anyway—approximately, tenderly, mostly.
